sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: A red blood cell holds about 270 million hemoglobin molecules.
source_title: Hemoglobin and heme products (Merck technical article)
note: Excerpt: '~270 million hemoglobin molecules' per cell (episode 1, c14). Sources range 250–300 million, so the product below is 1.0–1.2 billion. 'Passengers' are oxygen molecules, the capacity, not a count of what is aboard at every moment.

sentence: Room for about a billion passengers.
claim: Each hemoglobin carries up to four O₂ (one per heme): 270 million × 4 ≈ 1.08 billion O₂ per cell.
source_title: OpenStax Biology 2e, 39.4 Transport of Gases in Human Bodily Fluids
note: Excerpt: hemoglobin is 'made of four subunits'; 'each heme group that contains iron binds one oxygen molecule'. 270,000,000 × 4 = 1,080,000,000 (computed): 'about a billion'.

sentence: It's packed with one protein, hemoglobin: about two hundred and seventy million copies.
claim: A red blood cell holds about 270 million hemoglobin molecules; hemoglobin is the protein that fills it.
source_title: Hemoglobin and heme products (Merck technical article)
note: Same excerpt as c1. 'Packed with one protein' is the plain reading: hemoglobin makes up most of a red cell's protein (no nucleus, no organelles; episode 1, c2/c3).

sentence: Each one has four iron atoms, and each can hold an oxygen.
claim: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with a heme group whose iron can bind one O₂.
source_title: Hemoglobin: Oxygen transport in mammals (LibreTexts Chemistry, Saint Mary's College CHEM 342)
note: Excerpt: two α and two β subunits, 'each carries a heme group with an inorganic iron ion'; oxygen is bound at the iron of each heme. OpenStax Biology 2e 39.4 says the same (c2). Review fix: 'each can hold', not 'every iron grips' (an iron holds O₂ only when bound, and only as Fe²⁺).

sentence: The first oxygen struggles to board, but each one makes the next one easier.
claim: Hemoglobin binds O₂ cooperatively: binding of the first O₂ changes the protein's shape so the remaining sites bind more readily (a sigmoidal binding curve).
source_title: Overview of Hemoglobin's Structure/Function Relationships (UC Santa Barbara, MCDB biochemistry)
note: Search excerpts (UCSB overview; Berg, Biochemistry 8e §7.2 'Hemoglobin binds oxygen cooperatively'): 'the more oxygen is bound to hemoglobin, the easier it is for more oxygen to bind'; the first binds with difficulty, then a conformational change makes the next easier. 'Easier' = higher affinity (review fix: not 'faster'). The film shows each boarding a little sooner as staging, badged as an illustration.

sentence: Dark red at the start; full, it's bright red.
claim: Oxygenated hemoglobin (blood) is bright red; deoxygenated is darker red, because the two absorb light differently.
source_title: Hemoglobin: Oxygen transport in mammals (LibreTexts Chemistry, Saint Mary's College CHEM 342)
note: Excerpt: oxygenated blood appears bright red, deoxygenated darker; absorption near 540–542 nm vs 554 nm. Live Science: 'bright cherry red' leaving the lungs, 'much darker red' in veins.

sentence: Your veins look blue, so it's easy to guess the blood inside them is.
claim: Veins under the skin often look blue, and a common belief is that the blood in them is blue.
source_title: If blood is red, why do veins look bluish? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: the blue look 'is an illusion' caused by the skin layer over the vein; blood is always red. The line states the appearance and the wrong guess, then corrects it (WRITING.md: a wrong idea). Bible §9: how blue a vein looks depends on its depth and on skin tone; under darker skin veins often look green (Live Science).

claim: Human blood is never blue: it is bright red when oxygenated and darker red when not.
source_title: If blood is red, why do veins look bluish? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: 'blood is never blue'; leaving the lungs bright cherry red, returning through veins much darker red.

claim: Blood returning in the veins is a darker red than oxygen-rich arterial blood.
source_title: If blood is red, why do veins look bluish? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: blood leaving the lungs is bright cherry red; returning through veins it is much darker red.

sentence: Red light sinks in, and the vein swallows it, so less red comes back.
claim: Red light penetrates skin more deeply (to where veins lie) and is absorbed by the blood in the vein, while blue light is scattered back near the surface; so less red light returns from above the vein than from the tissue around it, and the vein looks bluish by contrast.
source_title: Computer science researchers help answer age-old medical question (University of Waterloo)
note: University of Waterloo (bible S11; Kienle et al. 1996 modelled it) and Live Science excerpt: red light reaches roughly 5–10 mm, 'where many veins are'; blue is mostly scattered and absorbed near the surface; the surrounding tissue reflects more red than the vein, so the brain reads the vein as blue. 'Swallows' = absorbs. The skin picture is an illustration and is badged so. How blue a vein looks depends on its depth and on skin tone (bible §9).

sentence: Your heart sends your blood back through your lungs about once a minute.
claim: At rest the heart pumps about 5 L a minute, about equal to the body's whole blood volume, so on average the blood makes a full loop (through the lungs) about once a minute.
source_title: NCBI Bookshelf NBK54473 (physiology textbook chapter on blood volume and cardiac output; title not seen, only the search excerpt)
note: Excerpt (NCBI Bookshelf NBK54473): normal blood volume is about equal to the amount of blood pumped from the heart each minute. Cardiac output ≈ 5 L/min, blood volume ≈ 5 L: 5 / 5 = about once a minute (computed). An average: not every drop takes the same route or time (the source's caveat); 'about' keeps it there.

claim: Each pass through the lungs, oxygen moves into the blood and fills hemoglobin's empty sites.
source_title: Pulmonary physiology: diffusion (Loyola University Chicago, Stritch School of Medicine, Lumen)
note: Same source as c17 (Loyola Lumen): gas equilibrates across the alveolocapillary membrane during the capillary transit. 'The empty seats': returning blood at rest still carries most of its oxygen (venous saturation commonly about 75%), so only the empty sites fill (review fix).

sentence: The blue is your skin's trick.
claim: The blue look of veins is an optical effect of light in skin and tissue, not the colour of the blood.
source_title: If blood is red, why do veins look bluish? (Live Science)
note: Excerpt: the blue look 'is an illusion' caused by the skin layer over the vein. Same mechanism as c10.

sentence: The red is a passenger count: brighter means fuller seats.
claim: The more of its hemoglobin carries O₂, the brighter red blood is; less O₂, darker red.
source_title: Hemoglobin: Oxygen transport in mammals (LibreTexts Chemistry, Saint Mary's College CHEM 342)
note: As c6: the more of its hemoglobin carries O₂, the brighter red. A metaphor for the colour change (review fix: not 'fuel'), not a measuring method; no talk of pulse oximeters (bible §9).

sentence: Meanwhile, as you watched, your blood handed your body about a cup of oxygen.
claim: An average adult at rest uses about 250 mL of O₂ a minute, delivered by the blood.
source_title: Oxygen flux (e-Learning Anaesthesia, Royal College of Anaesthetists / NHS e-Learning for Healthcare)
note: Excerpt (e-Learning Anaesthesia, 'Oxygen flux'): delivery about 1000 mL/min, 'resting consumption only 25% of this (250 mL/min)'. Vernier and others: 200–250 mL/min. The tally is 250/60 × t mL from frame 0; the line starts near 62 s, about 258 mL; a US cup is about 237 mL (computed: 'about a cup' holds from 50 s to 70 s, 208–292 mL, within ±25%).

sentence: In the fastest, it doesn't crawl; it jumps.
claim: In myelinated axons the action potential is regenerated only at the nodes of Ranvier and so appears to jump from node to node (saltatory conduction), reaching up to about 150 m/s, against 0.5–10 m/s in unmyelinated axons.
source_title: Purves et al., Neuroscience 2nd ed., Increased Conduction Velocity as a Result of Myelination (NCBI Bookshelf NBK10921)
note: Excerpt (NBK10921): action potentials are generated only at the nodes; current flows passively to the next node, where the cycle repeats; unmyelinated 0.5–10 m/s, myelinated up to 150 m/s. 'Jumps' is the textbook word (saltatory). Episode 3 tells it. Review fix: hedged to the fastest (myelinated) fibres; unmyelinated fibres do conduct continuously.

sentence: In about a quarter of a second.
claim: At rest a red cell spends about 0.75 s in a lung capillary, and O₂ exchange across the alveolar wall is normally complete in about the first 0.25 s.
source_title: Pulmonary physiology: diffusion (Loyola University Chicago, Stritch School of Medicine, Lumen)
note: Excerpt (Loyola Lumen): transit = 75 mL × 60 / 6000 mL/min = 0.75 s; 'Normally, gas equilibrations across the alveolocapillary membrane are complete in 0.25 sec. The safety factor ... is 0.5 sec or 2/3 of the cap length.' BioNumbers 101731 gives 0.75 s (Nunn). 'Board' = the blood's O₂ reaches equilibrium with the air in the alveoli; venous blood arrives partly loaded, so not every seat is empty on arrival. Review fix: 'the empty seats fill', not 'they board': returning blood at rest still carries most of its oxygen (venous saturation is commonly about 75%).

claim: At rest, blood returning in the veins (PO₂ about 40 mmHg) still has about 75% of hemoglobin's O₂ sites filled. Shown on screen: 'seats still full in returning blood: about 75%'.
source_title: Oxygen transport and the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (R. E. Klabunde, Cardiovascular Physiology Concepts)
note: Excerpt: 'at a venous PO2 of 40 mmHg, approximately 75% of the binding sites are occupied by O2'. A lecture source agrees (still about 75 percent saturated). An at-rest average; it differs by organ (StatPearls gives 37% for heart muscle, 92% for kidney). The on-screen readout says 'about'.

sentence: The red is a passenger count: brighter means fuller seats.
claim: Arterial blood leaving the lungs has about 97% of hemoglobin's O₂ sites filled, against about 75% in returning venous blood at rest. Shown on screen: seats full 75% → 97%.
source_title: Oxygen transport and the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (R. E. Klabunde, Cardiovascular Physiology Concepts)
note: Excerpt: arterial saturation 'roughly 97%' at a PO2 of about 100 mmHg; other sources round to 98%. The readout runs 75 → 97 % as the cells cross the air sac (computed span: about 22 points of the seats refill per pass at rest).
